name: self-shunt
intent: Let the test object itself play the collaborator: implement the small outgoing interface the system under test calls back on, install the test object as the collaborator, and record the SUT's calls in the test's own fields so the test method can assert on them without creating a separate double.
problem: A test needs a double for a collaborator whose whole contract is a callback interface -- an observer, listener, time provider, comparator or completion callback -- and the required behaviour is specific to this one test case: canned answers that only this test knows, or a record of the calls only this test asserts on. Writing a named double class for that adds a type, a file and a retrieval interface that nothing else uses, and a framework mock is ceremony for a callback that would fit in three lines on the test itself.
context: Unit tests where the system under test depends on a substitutable collaborator (constructor, setter or registration seam) and the observation point is an incoming call rather than a query: the collaborator interface is small and used by a single test case or test class, the test language offers interface, protocol, trait or structural conformance (or dynamic dispatch), and the double's behaviour is trivial enough to live beside the assertions. Typical when an interface was just introduced to make an indirect output observable, or when a callback must be captured so the test can drive an otherwise asynchronous API synchronously.
benefits: No extra type: the double is the test object, so a single-use collaborator costs no file, no class and no retrieval interface -- the smallest possible test double.
The callback can write straight into the test's own fields (and even assert inline), so the test method and the observation point share state by construction instead of through getters.

The dependency becomes explicit: in statically typed languages the test class must name the outgoing interface, which forces the observation seam to be visible and reviewable in the test's declaration.
The double is confined to the test that needs it -- no production code can accidentally use it, and no shared fixture invites reuse that would couple unrelated tests.
In dynamic languages the technique needs no declaration at all: passing self (or a bound method) as the collaborator is the direct expression of duck typing.

Works when the collaborator interface is required by the framework or the SUT signature and a mock framework cannot be introduced (no dependency, restrictive build, or a protocol the framework must satisfy).
tradeoffs: The test class takes on a second responsibility (implementing the collaborator contract), and it now changes for two reasons -- when the test changes and when the collaborator interface changes -- so every test in that class is recompiled and re-run on an interface edit.

Only small interfaces are affordable: a many-method collaborator forces placeholder implementations for calls the test never makes, and those placeholders fail late and obscurely when the SUT suddenly calls one of them.

The shunt is invisible as a double: unlike a named Mock Object with explicit expectations, nothing in the test announces that the test object is the collaborator, so a reader must spot the installation call to understand where the observed values come from.

It does not scale across tests: the behaviour is hard-coded per test class, so a second test class needing the same collaborator duplicates it (Meszaros' Test Code Duplication), which is why the pattern is a stepping stone to a Hard-Coded or Configurable Test Double.

Framework lifecycle can collide with the interface: callback method names may clash with fixture hooks or be picked up as tests by prefix-based runners, and the test object must implement the interface's members even when the framework also wants those names.

The test object's lifetime bounds the double: a SUT that retains the collaborator beyond the test (async delivery, long-lived publisher) can call back into a finished or torn-down test unless the test unregisters it.

participants.responsibility: The test case class or test-local object; it implements the outgoing interface of the collaborator, holds the recorded values in its own fields and is installed into the SUT as the depended-on component.
Depends on the collaborator interface, calls it at the observation point, and behaves exactly as it would with the real collaborator -- it cannot tell that the test object is standing in.

The small callback contract the SUT uses to report to or query its collaborator (Observer, listener, delegate, provider, comparator, completion callback); it defines exactly what the shunt must implement.
The substitutable dependency through which the test object replaces the real collaborator for the duration of the test -- constructor parameter, setter, add-listener registration or a factory.
Builds the fixture state, installs the shunt, exercises the SUT, and asserts on the shunt's recorded fields (or on the SUT's own results).

use_cases: Observing indirect outputs: the test implements the listener/observer interface and records the events the SUT publishes, then asserts the sequence and payloads after exercising it.

Controlling indirect inputs through a provider interface: the test method supplies the time, id or configuration the SUT asks for by implementing getTime()/nextId()/setting() on the test object and returning canned values.

Capturing a completion or continuation callback so an asynchronous API can be driven synchronously: the test stores the callback passed by the SUT and invokes it with the desired result inside the test.
Recording what an algorithm saw: the test implements a comparator, visitor or visitor-like callback and collects the elements in traversal order while the SUT runs.

Satisfying a collaborator contract the test framework or the SUT signature demands (a JUnit 3 Testcase Class that must also be the listener, an XCTestCase protocol witness, a test-local Go struct handed to a service).
Self-verifying observation: the callback asserts immediately inside the shunt method (mock-style), which keeps the failure at the point where the wrong call arrived instead of after the exercise.

Shunting a standard listener API instead of inventing a one-off interface: the test case implements java.beans.PropertyChangeListener, installs itself on the bean under test with addPropertyChangeListener(), and asserts on the PropertyChangeEvents it recorded once the bean's setter fires the bound-property change.

Registering the test object as a DOM event listener: EventTarget.addEventListener() accepts any object with a handleEvent() method (the WebIDL EventListener callback interface), so the test object adds itself to the element the component dispatches on and records the events in its own fields -- no closure, no separate double.

Recording executor completions in Python: concurrent.futures.Future.add_done_callback() takes any callable invoked with the future, so a test object whose __call__ appends to a test field is passed straight to add_done_callback() and the test asserts on the recorded futures after the work finishes.
avoid_when: More than one test class (or several unrelated tests) needs the same collaborator behaviour: extract a Hard-Coded Test Double class or a Configurable Test Double instead of duplicating the shunt.

The collaborator interface is large and the test observes one or two of its methods: a dedicated stub implementing only what matters, or a dynamic mock, avoids a pile of placeholder methods on the test class.
The collaborator's behaviour is nontrivial -- state machine, scripted responses, failure injection across scenarios: a configurable double or a framework mock keeps that logic out of the test class.

Only one test method needs the double and the language supports local types, lambdas or object expressions: an Inner Test Double declared inside the method reads better and leaves the test class clean.
The observation point is a query the test can call after exercise (a repository, a service, a data structure): a recording fake or spy is the natural double and no callback contract is needed.

The test class cannot implement the interface or is already loaded with fixture responsibilities (existing base class, sealed type, single-inheritance conflicts, framework lifecycle hooks): use a separate or inner double.
anti_patterns: Making the test class implement a large production interface to observe one callback: the fixture drowns in placeholder methods and every interface change touches the test.
Letting the shunt accumulate behaviour until the test class is a partial reimplementation of the collaborator, with the test now validating its own callback logic instead of the SUT.
Recording into module-level or static state so that one shunt serves several tests, which couples them and breaks under parallel or reordered execution.
Naming the callback method so that the test runner picks it up as a test (prefix-based discovery) or so that it overrides a fixture hook -- the shunt then runs, or blocks, at the wrong time.
Keeping a self shunt as the only double for a collaborator used by many tests, instead of promoting it to a configurable test double.
Forgetting to unregister the shunt from a long-lived subject, so callbacks fire into a finished test and either corrupt state or fail later in an unrelated test.
design_principles: Substitutability: the test object must honour the collaborator contract as far as the SUT can observe it -- the shunt is a real implementation, not a straw man.
Test through the published interface: implementing the outgoing interface makes the observation point explicit rather than reaching into the SUT's internals.
Single responsibility, deliberately traded: accept the second role while the double stays trivial, and escalate to a dedicated double when it grows -- Meszaros' variation is scoped to one test class.
Pragmatism over framework: use the object the test framework already gives you as the double when that is all the collaborator contract needs.
Keep test-specific behaviour close to the test: a double used once belongs beside its assertions, not in a shared fixture layer.
best_practices: Shunt only small, purpose-built interfaces, and only while a single test class (or a single test method, via a local implementation) needs the collaborator.
Keep callback bodies to recording or returning canned values; put the assertions in the test method, or assert inline only when the failure point matters more than the reading order.
Install the shunt through a real substitution seam (constructor/setter/registration) so the test also proves the SUT can be given a collaborator at all.
Reset or re-create the shunt state per test (fresh fields, setUp/tearDown or a fresh instance), and never record into static or module-level state.
Unregister or neutralise the shunt in tearDown when the SUT (or a subject it subscribes to) can outlive the test, and keep asynchronous callbacks from writing after the assertion.
Watch for the growth signal -- a second observed method, a second test class, behaviour instead of recording -- and promote the shunt to a hard-coded or configurable test double at that point.
Pair the shunt with at least one test against the real collaborator when the assumed callback contract matters, so the interface semantics are not only asserted through the test object.
sources: Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code, Chapter 23 'Test Double Patterns' - Self Shunt (variation of Hard-Coded Test Double and of Test Spy, p. 570), Addison-Wesley 2007.
